questions.q: Evaluate $\int \sin x\cos x\,dx$ two ways: (a) using $u=\sin x$, and (b) using the identity $\sin x\cos x=\frac{1}{2}\sin(2x)$. Confirm both give equivalent answers.
questions.target: Substitution with double angle and reciprocal forms
questions.answer: (a) $u=\sin x$: $\int u\,du=\frac{\sin^2x}{2}+C$. (b) $\int\frac{1}{2}\sin(2x)\,dx=-\frac{1}{4}\cos(2x)+C$. Using $\cos(2x)=1-2\sin^2x$: $-\frac{1}{4}(1-2\sin^2x)+C=\frac{\sin^2x}{2}+C'$ — the same family, differing only by the constant.
questions.explanation: (a) $u=\sin x$: $\int u\,du=\frac{\sin^2x}{2}+C$. (b) $\int\frac{1}{2}\sin(2x)\,dx=-\frac{1}{4}\cos(2x)+C$. Using $\cos(2x)=1-2\sin^2x$: $-\frac{1}{4}(1-2\sin^2x)+C=\frac{\sin^2x}{2}+C'$ — the same family, differing only by the constant.

questions.q: Use the substitution $x = 2\sin\theta$ to evaluate the exact definite integral $\int_0^1 \sqrt{4 - x^2}\,dx$.
questions.target: Substitution with radicals
questions.answer: 1. Substitute $x = 2\sin\theta \Rightarrow dx = 2\cos\theta\,d\theta$. When $x = 0$, $\theta = 0$. When $x = 1$, $2\sin\theta = 1 \Rightarrow \sin\theta = \frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \theta = \frac{\pi}{6}$. 2. Rewrite integrand: $\sqrt{4 - x^2} = \sqrt{4 - 4\sin^2\theta} = 2\sqrt{\cos^2\theta} = 2\cos\theta \quad (\mathrm{since\ } \cos\theta > 0 \mathrm{\ on\ } [0, \pi/6]).$ 3. Substitute into the integral: $\int_0^1 \sqrt{4 - x^2}\,dx = \int_0^{\pi/6} (2\cos\theta)(2\cos\theta\,d\theta) = 4 \int_0^{\pi/6} \cos^2\theta\,d\theta.$ 4. Use double-angle identity $\cos^2\theta = \frac{1 + \cos 2\theta}{2}$: $= 4 \int_0^{\pi/6} \frac{1 + \cos 2\theta}{2}\,d\theta = 2 \left[ \theta + \frac{\sin 2\theta}{2} \right]_0^{\pi/6} = 2\left( \frac{\pi}{6} + \frac{\sin(\pi/3)}{2} \right) = 2\left( \frac{\pi}{6} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} \right) = \frac{\pi}{3} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.$
questions.explanation: 1. Substitute $x = 2\sin\theta \Rightarrow dx = 2\cos\theta\,d\theta$. When $x = 0$, $\theta = 0$. When $x = 1$, $2\sin\theta = 1 \Rightarrow \sin\theta = \frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \theta = \frac{\pi}{6}$. 2. Rewrite integrand: $\sqrt{4 - x^2} = \sqrt{4 - 4\sin^2\theta} = 2\sqrt{\cos^2\theta} = 2\cos\theta \quad (\mathrm{since\ } \cos\theta > 0 \mathrm{\ on\ } [0, \pi/6]).$ 3. Substitute into the integral: $\int_0^1 \sqrt{4 - x^2}\,dx = \int_0^{\pi/6} (2\cos\theta)(2\cos\theta\,d\theta) = 4 \int_0^{\pi/6} \cos^2\theta\,d\theta.$ 4. Use double-angle identity $\cos^2\theta = \frac{1 + \cos 2\theta}{2}$: $= 4 \int_0^{\pi/6} \frac{1 + \cos 2\theta}{2}\,d\theta = 2 \left[ \theta + \frac{\sin 2\theta}{2} \right]_0^{\pi/6} = 2\left( \frac{\pi}{6} + \frac{\sin(\pi/3)}{2} \right) = 2\left( \frac{\pi}{6} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} \right) = \frac{\pi}{3} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.$

questions.q: Level 1 · FoundationsFind the area of the region bounded by $x = y^2$ and $x = y + 2$ using integration with respect to $y$.
questions.target: Visualizing an area found by substitution
questions.answer: Find intersections in terms of $y$: $y^2 = y + 2 \Rightarrow y^2 - y - 2 = 0 \Rightarrow (y - 2)(y + 1) = 0 \Rightarrow y = -1, \; y = 2$ For $y \in (-1, 2)$, test $y = 0$: $x_{\mathrm{line}} = 2 > x_{\mathrm{parabola}} = 0$. The right curve is $x = y + 2$ and the left curve is $x = y^2$. Integrate with respect to $y$: $A = \int_{-1}^2 \left[ (y + 2) - y^2 \right]\,dy = \left[ \frac{y^2}{2} + 2y - \frac{y^3}{3} \right]_{-1}^2$ At $y = 2$: $2 + 4 - \frac{8}{3} = 6 - \frac{8}{3} = \frac{10}{3}$. At $y = -1$: $\frac{1}{2} - 2 + \frac{1}{3} = -\frac{3}{2} + \frac{1}{3} = -\frac{7}{6}$. Subtracting: $A = \frac{10}{3} - \left(-\frac{7}{6}\right) = \frac{20}{6} + \frac{7}{6} = \mathbf{\frac{27}{6} = \frac{9}{2}} = 4.5.$
questions.explanation: Find intersections in terms of $y$: $y^2 = y + 2 \Rightarrow y^2 - y - 2 = 0 \Rightarrow (y - 2)(y + 1) = 0 \Rightarrow y = -1, \; y = 2$ For $y \in (-1, 2)$, test $y = 0$: $x_{\mathrm{line}} = 2 > x_{\mathrm{parabola}} = 0$. The right curve is $x = y + 2$ and the left curve is $x = y^2$. Integrate with respect to $y$: $A = \int_{-1}^2 \left[ (y + 2) - y^2 \right]\,dy = \left[ \frac{y^2}{2} + 2y - \frac{y^3}{3} \right]_{-1}^2$ At $y = 2$: $2 + 4 - \frac{8}{3} = 6 - \frac{8}{3} = \frac{10}{3}$. At $y = -1$: $\frac{1}{2} - 2 + \frac{1}{3} = -\frac{3}{2} + \frac{1}{3} = -\frac{7}{6}$. Subtracting: $A = \frac{10}{3} - \left(-\frac{7}{6}\right) = \frac{20}{6} + \frac{7}{6} = \mathbf{\frac{27}{6} = \frac{9}{2}} = 4.5.$

questions.q: Level 2 · MediumA 13-foot ladder leans against a vertical wall. The base of the ladder slides away from the wall at a constant rate of 2 ft/s. How fast is the top of the ladder sliding down the wall when the base is 5 feet from the wall?
questions.target: Substitution with double angle and reciprocal forms
questions.answer: Let $x$ be the distance from the base to the wall and $y$ be the height on the wall. By the Pythagorean theorem: $x^2 + y^2 = 13^2 = 169$ At the instant $x = 5$: $y = \sqrt{169 - 25} = \sqrt{144} = 12\mathrm{\ ft}$. Differentiating implicitly with respect to time $t$: $2x\frac{dx}{dt} + 2y\frac{dy}{dt} = 0 \Rightarrow x\frac{dx}{dt} + y\frac{dy}{dt} = 0$ Substitute $x = 5$, $y = 12$, and $\frac{dx}{dt} = 2\mathrm{\ ft/s}$: $(5)(2) + (12)\frac{dy}{dt} = 0 \Rightarrow 10 + 12\frac{dy}{dt} = 0 \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dt} = -\frac{10}{12} = -\mathbf{\frac{5}{6}\mathrm{\ ft/s}}.$ The top of the ladder is sliding down at a rate of $\frac{5}{6}\mathrm{\ ft/s}$ (approx. 0.833 ft/s).
questions.explanation: Let $x$ be the distance from the base to the wall and $y$ be the height on the wall. By the Pythagorean theorem: $x^2 + y^2 = 13^2 = 169$ At the instant $x = 5$: $y = \sqrt{169 - 25} = \sqrt{144} = 12\mathrm{\ ft}$. Differentiating implicitly with respect to time $t$: $2x\frac{dx}{dt} + 2y\frac{dy}{dt} = 0 \Rightarrow x\frac{dx}{dt} + y\frac{dy}{dt} = 0$ Substitute $x = 5$, $y = 12$, and $\frac{dx}{dt} = 2\mathrm{\ ft/s}$: $(5)(2) + (12)\frac{dy}{dt} = 0 \Rightarrow 10 + 12\frac{dy}{dt} = 0 \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dt} = -\frac{10}{12} = -\mathbf{\frac{5}{6}\mathrm{\ ft/s}}.$ The top of the ladder is sliding down at a rate of $\frac{5}{6}\mathrm{\ ft/s}$ (approx. 0.833 ft/s).

questions.q: Use the substitution $u = 2x + 1$ to find the exact value of $\int_0^4 \frac{x}{\sqrt{2x+1}}\,dx$.
questions.target: Substitution in motion and rate problems
questions.answer: Let $u = 2x + 1$, so $du = 2\,dx \Rightarrow dx = \frac{1}{2}\,du$, and $x = \frac{u - 1}{2}$. Change limits: $x = 0 \Rightarrow u = 1,\quad x = 4 \Rightarrow u = 9$ Transform the integral: $\int_0^4 \frac{x}{\sqrt{2x+1}}\,dx = \int_1^9 \frac{\frac{u - 1}{2}}{\sqrt{u}}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\,du = \frac{1}{4}\int_1^9 \left(u^{1/2} - u^{-1/2}\right)\,du$ $= \frac{1}{4}\left[ \frac{2}{3}u^{3/2} - 2u^{1/2} \right]_1^9 = \frac{1}{4}\left( \left(\frac{2}{3}(27) - 2(3)\right) - \left(\frac{2}{3}(1) - 2(1)\right) \right)$ $= \frac{1}{4}\left( (18 - 6) - \left(-\frac{4}{3}\right) \right) = \frac{1}{4}\left(12 + \frac{4}{3}\right) = \frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{40}{3}\right) = \frac{10}{3}$
questions.explanation: Let $u = 2x + 1$, so $du = 2\,dx \Rightarrow dx = \frac{1}{2}\,du$, and $x = \frac{u - 1}{2}$. Change limits: $x = 0 \Rightarrow u = 1,\quad x = 4 \Rightarrow u = 9$ Transform the integral: $\int_0^4 \frac{x}{\sqrt{2x+1}}\,dx = \int_1^9 \frac{\frac{u - 1}{2}}{\sqrt{u}}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\,du = \frac{1}{4}\int_1^9 \left(u^{1/2} - u^{-1/2}\right)\,du$ $= \frac{1}{4}\left[ \frac{2}{3}u^{3/2} - 2u^{1/2} \right]_1^9 = \frac{1}{4}\left( \left(\frac{2}{3}(27) - 2(3)\right) - \left(\frac{2}{3}(1) - 2(1)\right) \right)$ $= \frac{1}{4}\left( (18 - 6) - \left(-\frac{4}{3}\right) \right) = \frac{1}{4}\left(12 + \frac{4}{3}\right) = \frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{40}{3}\right) = \frac{10}{3}$

questions.q: Use trigonometric substitution to evaluate the indefinite integral $\int \frac{1}{(4 + x^2)^{3/2}}\,dx$.
questions.target: Recognizing when substitution simplifies a problem
questions.cross_lesson: 3.02 Differentiation Rules: Power, Product, Quotient, Chain
questions.answer: 1. Substitute $x = 2\tan\theta \Rightarrow dx = 2\sec^2\theta\,d\theta$. Then $4 + x^2 = 4 + 4\tan^2\theta = 4\sec^2\theta$, so: $(4 + x^2)^{3/2} = (4\sec^2\theta)^{3/2} = 8\sec^3\theta.$ 2. Substitute into the integral: $\int \frac{2\sec^2\theta}{8\sec^3\theta}\,d\theta = \frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sec\theta}\,d\theta = \frac{1}{4}\int \cos\theta\,d\theta = \frac{1}{4}\sin\theta + C.$ 3. Express $\sin\theta$ in terms of $x$: From $\tan\theta = \frac{x}{2}$, construct a right triangle with opposite side $x$, adjacent side 2, and hypotenuse $\sqrt{x^2 + 4}$. Thus $\sin\theta = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + 4}}$. Final Result: $\frac{x}{4\sqrt{x^2 + 4}} + C.$
questions.explanation: 1. Substitute $x = 2\tan\theta \Rightarrow dx = 2\sec^2\theta\,d\theta$. Then $4 + x^2 = 4 + 4\tan^2\theta = 4\sec^2\theta$, so: $(4 + x^2)^{3/2} = (4\sec^2\theta)^{3/2} = 8\sec^3\theta.$ 2. Substitute into the integral: $\int \frac{2\sec^2\theta}{8\sec^3\theta}\,d\theta = \frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sec\theta}\,d\theta = \frac{1}{4}\int \cos\theta\,d\theta = \frac{1}{4}\sin\theta + C.$ 3. Express $\sin\theta$ in terms of $x$: From $\tan\theta = \frac{x}{2}$, construct a right triangle with opposite side $x$, adjacent side 2, and hypotenuse $\sqrt{x^2 + 4}$. Thus $\sin\theta = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + 4}}$. Final Result: $\frac{x}{4\sqrt{x^2 + 4}} + C.$

questions.q: Level 3 · AdvancedLet $R$ be the region bounded by $y = \sqrt{x}$, $y = 2$, and the y-axis. Set up, but do not evaluate, an integral for the volume generated when $R$ is revolved about the vertical line $x = -1$.
questions.target: u-substitution
questions.answer: 1. The region has boundaries $x = y^2$ (right boundary), $x = 0$ (left boundary / y-axis), and $y$ runs from $y = 0$ to $y = 2$. 2. The axis of rotation is the vertical line $x = -1$. Slicing perpendicular to the axis of rotation requires integration with respect to $y$ (horizontal washers). 3. Determine outer and inner radii:Outer radius (distance from $x = -1$ to furthest curve $x = y^2$): $R(y) = y^2 - (-1) = y^2 + 1$ Inner radius (distance from $x = -1$ to closer curve $x = 0$): $r(y) = 0 - (-1) = 1$ 4. Set up the washer volume integral: $V = \mathbf{\pi \int_0^2 \left( (y^2 + 1)^2 - 1 \right)\,dy} = \pi \int_0^2 (y^4 + 2y^2)\,dy.$
questions.explanation: 1. The region has boundaries $x = y^2$ (right boundary), $x = 0$ (left boundary / y-axis), and $y$ runs from $y = 0$ to $y = 2$. 2. The axis of rotation is the vertical line $x = -1$. Slicing perpendicular to the axis of rotation requires integration with respect to $y$ (horizontal washers). 3. Determine outer and inner radii:Outer radius (distance from $x = -1$ to furthest curve $x = y^2$): $R(y) = y^2 - (-1) = y^2 + 1$ Inner radius (distance from $x = -1$ to closer curve $x = 0$): $r(y) = 0 - (-1) = 1$ 4. Set up the washer volume integral: $V = \mathbf{\pi \int_0^2 \left( (y^2 + 1)^2 - 1 \right)\,dy} = \pi \int_0^2 (y^4 + 2y^2)\,dy.$

questions.q: Level 2 · MediumFind the angle(s) $\theta \in [0, \pi]$ at which the polar curve $r = 3\cos\theta$ passes through the origin, and determine the equation of the tangent line at that point.
questions.target: Definite integrals with substitution
questions.answer: Set $r = 0$: $3\cos\theta = 0 \Rightarrow \theta = \frac{\pi}{2}.$ By the Tangents at the Pole Theorem, when $r(\theta_0) = 0$ and $r'(\theta_0) eq 0$, the line $\theta = \theta_0$ is the tangent line. Thus, the tangent line at the pole is $\mathbf{\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}}$ (the vertical line $x = 0$).
questions.explanation: Set $r = 0$: $3\cos\theta = 0 \Rightarrow \theta = \frac{\pi}{2}.$ By the Tangents at the Pole Theorem, when $r(\theta_0) = 0$ and $r'(\theta_0) eq 0$, the line $\theta = \theta_0$ is the tangent line. Thus, the tangent line at the pole is $\mathbf{\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}}$ (the vertical line $x = 0$).
